summary: Specifies using the elliptic curves Curve25519 and Curve448 for the ephemeral key exchange in IKEv2, the key negotiation protocol used by IPsec VPNs. These curves are widely used modern choices for key agreement.

plainLanguage.summary: Two people want to agree on a secret color while others watch. This lets VPN software use two modern math tricks to do it safely.

questions: how big is the curve25519 shared secret
subtitle: Two modern elliptic curves, Curve25519 and Curve448, become key exchange groups for IKEv2 VPN negotiation.

tldr.problem: IKEv2 only had the older NIST elliptic curves for Diffie-Hellman key exchange. Newer curves are faster and easier to implement in constant time, which resists timing side-channel attacks.
tldr.mechanism: Each side computes a public key with the X25519 or X448 function from RFC 7748 and swaps it in the Key Exchange payload. The result is a 32-octet or 56-octet shared secret, negotiated as Diffie-Hellman group 31 or 32.
tldr.outcome: IKEv2 peers can now agree on keys with Curve25519 or Curve448. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 8031 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2016, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of using Curve25519 and Curve448 as IKEv2 Diffie-Hellman groups 31 and 32.

sections.title: Why Add New Curves to IKEv2
sections.content:
RFC 7748 describes two elliptic curves, Curve25519 and Curve448, along with the X25519 and X448 functions for Diffie-Hellman key agreement. This RFC brings them into the Internet Key Exchange Protocol Version 2 (IKEv2) from RFC 7296.

Elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman had been specified for IKEv2 for almost ten years, in RFC 5903 and its predecessor, using the so-called NIST curves. The RFC argues that the state of the art has moved on: more modern curves allow faster implementations and make it much easier to write constant-time code that resists time-based side-channel attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: The old way of mixing secrets worked, but newer recipes are faster and harder to trip up. This RFC teaches VPN software the new recipes.

sections.title: How the Key Exchange Works
sections.content:
Implementations SHALL use the X25519 and X448 functions from RFC 7748 for all computations. Parameters such as the base point, and the encoding details (pruning the least and most significant bits, little-endian encoding), also follow RFC 7748.

The exchange is ephemeral Diffie-Hellman. Each party picks a secret key d uniformly at random and computes its public key as pub_mine = X(d, G), where X is X25519 or X448 and G is the matching base point. The parties swap public keys and compute SHARED_SECRET = X(d, pub_peer).

The shared secret is used directly as the value called g^ir in Section 2.14 of RFC 7296. It is 32 octets for Curve25519 and 56 octets for Curve448.
sections.plainLanguage: Each friend keeps a private number and shares a public one. Mixing your private number with your friend's public one gives you both the same secret, and watchers cannot work it out.

sections.title: Negotiating the Curves in IKEv2
sections.content:
The curves are negotiated like any other Diffie-Hellman group: as Transform Type 4 in the Security Association (SA) payload of an IKE_SA_INIT or CREATE_CHILD_SA exchange.

Group number 31 stands for Curve25519 and 32 for Curve448.
sections.plainLanguage: When two computers start talking, they agree on which recipe to use. Number 31 means the smaller curve and 32 means the bigger one.

sections.title: The Key Exchange Payload
sections.content:
The RFC reuses the Key Exchange payload layout from Section 3.4 of RFC 7296 and fixes the values for the new groups.

  • Payload Length: 40 for Curve25519 (a 32-octet public key) and 64 for Curve448 (a 56-octet public key).
  • Diffie-Hellman Group Num: 31 for Curve25519 or 32 for Curve448.
  • Key Exchange Data: the 32 or 56 octets described in Section 6 of RFC 7748.
sections.plainLanguage: The message has a label saying which recipe was used, and then the public number itself. The label and the length have to match the curve.

sections.title: Recipient Tests
sections.content: Receivers must handle incompatible point formats as described in Section 5 of RFC 7748. In particular, receiving entities MUST mask the most-significant bit in the final byte for X25519 (but not for X448), and implementations MUST accept non-canonical values.
sections.plainLanguage: When a public number arrives, you tidy one particular bit in a specific way for the small curve, and you accept numbers even if they are written in an unusual form.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Both curves are designed to make high-performance constant-time implementations easy. Implementors are encouraged to use constant-time code, and the RFC calls this crucial, especially if an implementation reuses its ephemeral key pair across many key exchanges for performance.

Curve25519 targets about a 128-bit security level, comparable to the 256-bit random ECP group 19 (NIST P-256) from RFC 5903. Curve448 targets about 224 bits.

The RFC also contrasts how the curves were chosen. The NIST curves are advertised as chosen verifiably at random, yet there is no explanation for the seeds. The process behind Curve25519 and Curve448 is fully documented, so independent verification can be done, which prevents the generating party from maliciously manipulating the parameters. The Brainpool curves of RFC 6954 are also verifiably generated, but brainpoolP256 (group 28) is significantly slower than NIST P-256, which is itself slower than Curve25519.
sections.plainLanguage: The new recipes were made in the open, so anyone can check nothing sneaky is hidden. They are also built so a spy cannot learn secrets by timing how long the computer takes.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA assigned two values in the IKEv2 registry "Transform Type 4 - Diffie-Hellman Group Transform IDs": number 31 for Curve25519 and 32 for Curve448. Both entries point to RFC 8031 as the reference, and their Recipient Tests field points to Section 3.2 of this document.
sections.plainLanguage: A librarian wrote the two new recipe numbers into the official list, so everyone uses the same numbers.

sections.title: Numerical Example
sections.content:
Appendix A walks through a Curve25519 exchange. Initiator and responder each generate 32 random octets, then fix them by unsetting some bits as RFC 7748 describes, which affects only the first and last octets. The fixed values are read as little-endian private keys. Public keys come from X25519(d, G), and both sides end up with the same 32-octet SHARED_SECRET.

The example was calculated using the master version of OpenSSL, retrieved on August 4th, 2016.
sections.plainLanguage: The appendix shows a full worked example with real numbers, so people building this can check that their answer matches.
